Findings.Comment: `totalWithVat` converts the cent-valued subtotal into euros (`subtotal(lines) / 100`), scales it by the VAT factor, and converts back — floating-point euro arithmetic on money, which B1 forbids end to end. On a realistic cart this also loses precision: e.g. a subtotal of 1000 cents with `vatRate = 0.21` yields `gross = 12.100000000000001` euros, so `(gross * 100) as Cents` produces a non-integer cent value (1210.0000000000002) cast to `Cents`, and other amounts round off by a cent. Keep the value in `Cents` and scale in cents.
Findings.Headline: totalWithVat does VAT math on floating-point euros

Expected.why: The total is computed in floating-point euros and returned unrounded as Cents, which the blocking rule forbids and which yields fractional cents.

Findings.Comment: The new log line writes the customer's `Email` and `IBAN` straight into the application log on every successful create. Both are personal data covered by the project's blocking rule against logging personal data, and request-derived values like these typically end up in centralized log storage with broad read access, so a single `POST /customers` with a valid payload leaks the customer's contact and bank details into the log pipeline.
Findings.Headline: Customer create logs email and IBAN personal data

Expected.why: The success log carries the customer's email and IBAN, which the blocking rule forbids.

Findings.Comment: The new `/orders/{id}/lines` endpoint queries the database straight from `OrderController` via `JdbcTemplate.queryForList(...)`, and the controller now depends on `JdbcTemplate` directly. The project's blocking rule requires every query to go through a service — the neighbouring `get(...)` method already shows the sanctioned pattern (`orders.find(id)`). On any request to `/orders/{id}/lines`, the SQL runs in the controller layer, bypassing `OrderService` and any of its transaction/validation/business rules.
Findings.Headline: Controller queries the database directly via JdbcTemplate
Evidence: public List<Map<String, Object>> lines(@PathVariable long id) {
return jdbc.queryForList("SELECT sku, qty FROM order_lines WHERE order_id = ?", id);

Expected.why: The new endpoint queries order_lines from the controller, which the blocking rule forbids. A reviewer may anchor on the query (29), the method (28) or the injected field (15).

Findings.Comment: The new `Get` handler loads an invoice by id via `h.Store.Invoice(r.Context(), r.PathValue("id"))` and returns it without ever calling `authz.SameTenant(r, inv.TenantID)`. Any authenticated caller who can guess or enumerate another tenant's invoice id receives that tenant's invoice data — a direct cross-tenant data leak on the happy path. The project guideline makes this check mandatory in every handler that loads an invoice by id.
Findings.Headline: Get handler returns invoice without tenant ownership check

Expected.why: Get returns any invoice by id to any caller; the blocking rule demands authz.SameTenant first. Anchors anywhere from the signature (25) to the encode (31) are honest.

Findings.Comment: Removing the end clamp makes `page` slice past the end of `items` whenever the last page is partial. For a 3-item slice with `n=2, size=2`, `start` is 2 and passes the `start >= len(items)` guard, then `items[start : start+size]` evaluates `items[2:4]`, which panics with slice bounds out of range. Any caller paging until it sees an empty page hits this on every non-multiple total.
Findings.Headline: Last partial page panics: slice end is not clamped to len(items)

Expected.why: Without the clamp, start+size passes len(items) on a partial last page and the slice expression panics. No blocking rule covers it.

Findings.Comment: The retry gate is inverted: `retryable(lastErr)` is true for transient failures (network errors, 5xx, 429, 408), so those are returned immediately and never retried, while permanent rejections (4xx marked `ErrPermanent`) fall through to the retry loop and are retried up to `maxAttempts`. Delivering to an endpoint that returns 503 for one attempt now fails at once instead of backing off and retrying, and an endpoint that returns 410 is hammered with 5 requests despite `ErrPermanent` documented as "the same request would be rejected again". The nearby log line "will retry" also only ever fires for the non-retryable case.
Findings.Headline: Retry condition inverted: transient failures return, permanent ones retry

Expected.why: Transient failures such as a 503 are now returned on the first attempt without any retry, while permanently rejected deliveries are retried five times with backoff.

Findings.Comment: `FetchDiff` now builds its request and calls `getTextCapped` with `context.Background()` instead of the caller's `ctx`, so the caller's deadline and cancellation no longer apply to the diff fetch. A client that cancels the operation (request aborted, shutdown, upstream timeout) will leave the HTTP round trip and body read running until the transport's own timeout, contradicting the function's own contract on line 10 that "The caller's context bounds the whole operation, including the body read."
Findings.Headline: FetchDiff ignores the caller's context for the request and body read
Evidence: // The caller's context bounds the whole operation, including the body read.
func (c *Client) FetchDiff(ctx context.Context, project, repo string, pr int) (string, error) {

Expected.why: ctx is a parameter but never used; context.Background() is passed to both NewRequestWithContext and getTextCapped, so the caller's timeout and cancellation cannot stop the request or the body read. Bitbucket has no Client.Timeout by design, which makes the caller's ctx the only bound on a 10 MiB diff.

Findings.Comment: `Hold` now feeds `store.Touch`, whose parameter this PR changed to `ttlMillis` (it goes to Redis `PExpire`), with `int64(d.Seconds())` — a value in seconds. A hold of 30s therefore sets a TTL of 30 milliseconds, so the session key expires almost immediately during a long-running export and the user's session is gone well before the export finishes; a hold under one second truncates to 0 and comes back as `session: touch ...: non-positive ttl 0ms`. The rest of the PR converted `idleTTL` with `idle.Milliseconds()`, so this call site is the one left on the old unit.
Findings.Headline: Hold passes seconds to a millisecond TTL and drops the session

Expected.why: Touch now takes milliseconds, so a hold of two hours sets a lifetime of 7.2 seconds and the session expires while the export it was meant to cover is still running.

Findings.Comment: The `range` stop was changed from `len(items)` to `len(items) - size`, which drops the tail of the input. With `chunk([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2)` the loop runs for `i = 0, 2` only and returns `[[1, 2], [3, 4]]`, silently losing `[5]` — directly contradicting the module docstring, which documents `[[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]` for exactly that call. Worse, when `len(items)` is an exact multiple of `size` (e.g. `chunk([1, 2, 3, 4], 2)`) the range is empty and the function returns `[]`, so `batches()` yields nothing and an export run with a full batch boundary emits zero rows while appearing to succeed.
Findings.Headline: chunk() drops the trailing partial batch and full-batch inputs
Findings.Suggestion: return [items[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(items), size)]
Evidence: """Split items into lists of at most size elements."""
return [items[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(items) - size, size)]

Expected.why: range(0, len(items) - size, size) stops one step early: for five items and size 2 it yields starts 0 and 2 only, so [5] is lost, and for four items [3, 4] is. batches() hands every export through chunk, so the last rows of every export never reach the API. The module docstring's own example says the tail chunk is kept.

Findings.Comment: This diff adds a hardcoded plaintext password for the reporting datasource in the committed `application.yaml`. Unlike the primary datasource above it, which resolves `INVENTORY_DB_PASSWORD` from the environment at runtime, this literal is baked into the repository, so anyone with read access to the source (or any artifact built from it, e.g. the packaged jar) obtains the reporting database credential. Default-looking values such as `admin123` count as committed secrets and must not be checked in.
Findings.Headline: Hardcoded reporting datasource password committed in application.yaml

Expected.why: The reporting replica's password is committed in the application config, readable by everyone with repository access, while the existing datasource takes its password from the environment.

Findings.Comment: The new `password` field is initialized with the literal credential `admin123` and is passed straight to `reportingDataSource()`, which hands it to `HikariConfig.setPassword()`. The class javadoc states credentials are injected by the platform at deploy time, and the inventory pool follows that via `@Value("${INVENTORY_DB_PASSWORD}")`, so this literal is a real committed credential rather than a placeholder — anyone with repo or artifact read access can log in to the reporting replica as `reporting`. The hardcoded `reportingUrl` and `reportingUser` fields compound this by baking environment-specific connection data into source.
Findings.Headline: Hardcoded reporting DB password committed in DataSourceConfig
Evidence: return pool("reporting", reportingUrl, reportingUser, password, 4, true);

Expected.why: The reporting replica's password is committed in source, readable by everyone with repository access, while the class's own pattern reads credentials from the environment.

Findings.Comment: `Delete` reads and writes `c.items` without taking `c.mu`, while `Set` and `Get` both hold the mutex for every map access. With two goroutines using the cache concurrently — one calling `Delete` while another calls `Set` or `Get` — Go's runtime detects a concurrent map read and map write and throws `fatal error: concurrent map read and map write`, killing the whole process. This is the only method on the type that touches the map unlocked.
Findings.Headline: Delete mutates the cache map without holding the mutex
Findings.Suggestion:
func (c *Cache) Delete(key string) bool {
	c.mu.Lock()
	defer c.mu.Unlock()
	_, ok := c.items[key]
	delete(c.items, key)
	return ok
}

Expected.why: Delete touches c.items without c.mu while Set and Get hold it: a data race, and Go aborts the process on a concurrent map write.

Findings.Comment: `sourceAccountId` and `requesterAccountId` are both `Long`, so `!=` compares object references, not numeric values. Java caches boxed `Long`s only in the -128..127 range: for account ids above that (any realistic production id), the two boxes are distinct objects even when the values are equal, so the check reports a mismatch and the legitimate owner gets a `TransferAccessDeniedException` on every cancellation of their own transfer. Use `equals` (or compare primitives via `longValue()`) so the ownership check is value-based.
Findings.Headline: Ownership check in cancel() compares Long ids by reference

Expected.why: Boxed Longs are compared by reference, so for any account id above 127 the owner's own cancellation is rejected as access denied.

Findings.Comment: Removing `defer r.mu.Unlock()` and unlocking only at the end of the success path leaves the mutex locked on the early return for an unknown team. Any call such as `Disable("typo-slug", "reason")` returns the error while still holding `r.mu`, so every subsequent method that takes `r.mu` (including further `Disable` calls) blocks forever. The unlock must cover all return paths, not just the successful one.
Findings.Headline: Registry.Disable leaks the mutex lock on the unknown-team return

Expected.why: The Unlock now runs only on the success path, so returning the unknown-team error leaves r.mu locked and every subsequent caller blocks forever.

Findings.Comment: The nil-ticket branch now does nothing and execution falls through to `r.Ticket.Key`. In Go, `r.Ticket` is a `*Ticket`, so any `Result` with a nil `Ticket` — the case the removed guard existed for — dereferences a nil pointer at `r.Ticket.Key` and panics instead of returning the body alone. Every call to `Summarize` with a `Result` that has no linked ticket now crashes.
Findings.Headline: Summarize nil-dereferences Ticket after removing the nil guard's return
Evidence: // Ticket is optional; fall through to the shared renderer.

Expected.why: The nil branch no longer returns, so r.Ticket.Key panics whenever Ticket is nil. A reviewer may anchor on the dead check (19) or on the dereference (22).

Findings.Comment: Clamping `last` to `len(lines) + 1` sets `last` one past the end of the slice, so `return lines[first:last]` panics with a slice-bounds error whenever the trailing window reaches the end of the file — the very case this code exists to handle. Concrete path: `lines` with 5 elements, `h = Hunk{Start: 0, Count: 2}`, `n = 3` gives `first = 2`, `last = 5`; `5 >= 5` triggers the new clamp, `last` becomes 6, `first < last`, and `lines[2:6]` panics. It also contradicts the doc comment above the function, which states the window must stop at the last line of the file.
Findings.Headline: ContextAfter slices one past end of file and panics

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

Findings.Comment: The `defer resp.Body.Close()` that released the `whoami` response is gone, so `c.http.Do(req)` now hands back a body no one closes on any path — success included. Every call leaks the underlying connection and its read buffer: a script or service calling `WhoAmI` in a loop exhausts file descriptors and stalls once the transport's idle pool fills, and on the non-2xx path the body is also left unread, preventing connection reuse. The close must happen as soon as `err == nil`.
Findings.Headline: WhoAmI never closes the response body

Expected.why: The response body is never closed on any path, so the underlying connection is leaked on every call, successful or not.

Findings.Comment: Removing the lock around `q.depth = len(q.pending)` in `worker` leaves the depth counter written without synchronization while `Submit` and `Depth` access it under `q.mu`. In any deployment where a review is running while a caller submits or polls the backlog (the normal case, since `Submit` is documented as non-blocking), the worker's write races with those reads and writes: `Depth()` can return a torn/stale value, `Submit`'s `q.depth = len(q.pending)` can be overwritten by a stale `len(q.pending)` computed concurrently, and the read of `q.pending` races with `append` in `Submit`. This is a data race with undefined behavior under the Go memory model and will fail `go test -race`.
Findings.Headline: Backlog depth written in worker without holding q.mu

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: `getRates` wraps `return this.refresh(base)` in `try/catch`, but `refresh` is `async`: it returns a rejected promise instead of throwing synchronously, so the statement completes normally and the `catch` block never runs for a provider failure. In exactly the scenario this change targets — provider outage with a cached but expired table — the rejection propagates out of `getRates`, callers still fail, `staleServedCount` stays 0, and the warn log is never written. The refresh promise must be awaited inside the `try` for the rejection to reach the `catch`.
Findings.Headline: Stale-rate fallback never runs: try/catch misses the rejected refresh promise

Expected.why: The rejected promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs and a provider outage fails every request instead of serving the expired table.

Findings.Comment: `AddClaim` now discards the error returned by `tx.Commit(ctx)` and always returns `nil`. When the commit fails (serialization failure, connection drop, deferred constraint violation, server-side error), the `team_claims` row is rolled back by the deferred `tx.Rollback`, but the caller is told the claim was recorded. Any caller that proceeds on success — caching the claim, reporting ownership, skipping a retry — ends up acting on data that was never persisted.
Findings.Headline: Commit error discarded, AddClaim reports success on failed writes

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: The two error-wrapping branches are swapped relative to the documented contract. With this code, a query that finds no row for `project` returns an error wrapping the raw driver `err` (so `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` is `false`), while an actual database fault returns an error wrapping `ErrNoClaim` (so `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` is `true`). A caller that checks `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` to decide "unclaimed, safe to claim" will treat a transient DB failure as "nobody owns it" and proceed to claim, and will treat a genuinely unclaimed project as a hard failure. The doc comment on `ErrNoClaim` ("what callers match on when a project has no owner yet") states the opposite mapping.
Findings.Headline: Owner() wraps ErrNoClaim on DB faults instead of missing rows

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.
